Yes

This is a narrow, reversible three-card experiment tied to a concrete product cost and measurable outcome. It preserves stop-the-line behavior, keeps accountability with existing roles, and lets the task force decide retention at retro. The “unrun” path avoids forcing premature certainty, while its required fallback keeps slices honest. Counter-metrics guard against ceremony, so this returns quickly to product value without recreating D186’s up-front probe.

round1.cite: a numeric claim that carries its command cannot be wrong unseen
round1.reply:
Support-it
This is the right minimal lever: it narrows to numeric claims, keeps the existing D158 checklist, and avoids the broader D186 probe/table burden. It directly addresses the failure mode seen in card 264: an unverified “4 rows” claim caused a stopped green and a scope window. It is enforceable by a checklist rule and a missing-command block. The main caveat is governance: scope-window cap/category handling should remain explicit, but that’s a small tuning issue, not a reason to reject the pick.

round1.cite: a slice states a count, size or row number only with the command and output that produced it
round1.reply:
Support-it

The rule can be tested red first. Replay card 264's slice against the checklist: the "four rows" claim has no command, so the window blocks. That is a concrete failing case.

Two weaknesses remain. Nothing verifies that the pasted output was really run on HEAD, so a stale or invented output would pass. "Each numeric claim" also depends on the facilitator spotting every number, and that is a judgment call. Counter-metric 3 will show whether the checklist misses any, and the trial is cheap and reversible.

round1.cite: a slice states a count, size or row number only with the command and output that produced it
round1.reply:
Support-it

The trial is bounded, reversible, and hard to game because “unrun” requires both a reason and fallback behavior. Commands on committed HEAD make row, test, file, and call-site counts reproducible before green. The checklist gate adds modest overhead and fairly assigns correction to the architect. However, “each numeric claim” should be interpreted as testable delivery premises, excluding identifiers, policy references, caps, and estimates; durations also need environment context to remain meaningful.

round1.cite: slice checklist lists the numeric claims it found
round1.reply:
Support-it

Git can verify part of this. The checklist is committed before the window, so a missing claim-to-command line shows up in history. The slice lines are also committed, so their presence can be checked.

Git cannot verify that the quoted output came from committed HEAD. A pasted output block can be stale or hand-typed, and nothing in the proposal ties it to a commit hash.

"unrun: <reason>" is also an easy way to pass. The cap of two per slice is only a counter-metric, not a gate.

I would like the slice line to record the HEAD short hash the command ran on, and a hard cap on "unrun" claims. The trial is two-way and cheap, so I support it.
